speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. I see you are an infant presenting with recurrent stridor and wheezing; to start, is this breathing difficulty worse when you cry, eat, or exercise? REQUEST TEST: Pulse_Oximetry

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Pulse Oximetry not performed; clinical assessment indicates tachycardia (110 bpm) and tachypnea (30 breaths/min) with signs of respiratory distress including intercostal retractions and wheezing.

speaker: Patient
text: 10-month-old boy. The patient has been experiencing recurrent episodes of stridor and wheezing. The mother notes that the wheezing exacerbates when the child is crying, feeding, and when his neck is flexed. Additionally, there are instances where the child vomits after feeding.

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Recurrent episodes of stridor and wheezing. I also have Exacerbation during crying, Exacerbation during feeding, Exacerbation with neck flexion, Relief with neck extension, Occasional vomiting post-feeding. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Multiple sclerosis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Laryngomalacia (with possible co-existing tracheomalacia or vascular ring). The patient's classic symptoms—stridor worsening with crying and feeding, and specifically relief upon neck extension—are highly characteristic of laryngomalacia. The previous suggestion of Multiple Sclerosis is clinically implausible for an infant and must be disregarded. REQUEST TEST: Laryngoscopy; REQUEST IMAGES: Neck_Ultrasound (to rule out vascular compression).
